title: "I Remember That Question: How Prequestions Shape Reading"

    conflict-of-interest: The author has no conflicts of interest to disclose.

abstract: "Answering questions before a learning episode (prequestions) improves memory for the information the questions address, but why it does so is not well understood. One proposal is that prequestions guide attention toward the information they address. We tested this selective-attention account by recording eye movements while participants read a passage about efforts to eradicate polio and tuberculosis (TB). Before reading, participants answered prequestions about polio, prequestions about TB, or no prequestions; afterwards, all participants took a short-answer test on both topics. Prequestions produced a specific memory benefit—better memory than the no-prequestion condition for the prequestioned topic—but no general benefit for the non-prequestioned topic. Compared with the same sentences read without prequestions, sentences that answered a reader's prequestions received more occasional unusually long readings, were re-read more, and were more likely to be looked back to later, whereas typical reading time did not change. Non-prequestioned sentences were read largely as they were without prequestions. Prequestions thus guide attention selectively, but heightened attention is not the whole story: rather than slowing reading of the relevant material overall, they lead readers to pause on the answers and return to them, consistent with additional processing when readers recognize an answer to their prequestions."
keywords: [prequestions, pretesting, eye tracking, reading, attention, learning]

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
# REPRODUCIBILITY ---------------------------------------------------------------------
# Every number, table and figure in this manuscript is computed when the document is
# rendered. This chunk runs the shared setup and data (R/setup.R, R/data.R), using the
# eye-tracking measures derived from the fixation data by derive_et_measures.R, and a few
# helpers (R/manuscript_helpers.R). The Bayesian models reported in the paper are fitted
# in analysis/bayes_status.qmd, whose results file (analysis/bayes_results.rds) is read
# below. Nothing below is typed in by hand.
#
# Order of the pipeline (from raw data; run it all with targets::tar_make()):
#   1. grade_prequestions.R, grade_test.R  -> data/derived/preq_scored_*.csv, data/derived/test_scored_*.csv
#   2. derive_et_measures.R                -> data/derived/*.tsv
#   3. analysis/bayes_status.qmd           -> analysis/bayes_results.rds (Bayesian models)
#   4. scripts/manuscript_inputs.R          -> data/derived/manuscript_inputs.rds
#   5. this file (reads the results, then writes the paper)
params <- list(measures = "derived")
source(here::here("R", "setup.R"), local = knitr::knit_global())
# Everything below is read from files written by earlier targets; nothing is refitted or
# recomputed here. Sample, exclusions, calibration, materials and fixation-processing
# numbers: scripts/manuscript_inputs.R -> data/derived/manuscript_inputs.rds
list2env(readRDS(here::here("data", "derived", "manuscript_inputs.rds")), envir = knitr::knit_global())
# Agreement between the automated scoring and the second rater: scripts/rater_agreement.R
rater <- readRDS(here::here("data", "derived", "rater_agreement.rds"))
img2 <- png::readPNG(here::here("stimuli", "pages", "page2_full.png"))
# Functions: text helpers, page figures, path diagram
source(here::here("R", "manuscript_helpers.R"), local = knitr::knit_global())

# R packages used for the reported results (grading, measure derivation, Bayesian
# models, manuscript); their versions are read at render time
pipeline_packages <- c("tidyverse", "janitor", "png", "modelbased", "marginaleffects",
                       "insight", "brms", "cmdstanr", "cogmod", "ordbetareg", "bayestestR",
                       "priorsense", "ggdist", "quanteda", "quanteda.textstats", "udpipe",
                       "patchwork", "scales", "knitr", "xfun")
pkg_versions <- paste0(pipeline_packages, " ",
                       map_chr(pipeline_packages, \(p) as.character(packageVersion(p))))

# references are always those of the installed packages
knitr::write_bib(c("base", pipeline_packages), file = here::here("manuscript", "packages.bib"))
# udpipe's citation metadata braces a person's name ("{Milan Straka}"), which citeproc
# then treats as an organisation; write it as a person's name
writeLines(sub("{Milan Straka}", "Milan Straka", readLines(here::here("manuscript", "packages.bib")), fixed = TRUE),
           here::here("manuscript", "packages.bib"))
# Citation key per package: the package's preferred reference (from citation()) where
# it has one, otherwise its manual (R-<package>)
cite_key <- c(tidyverse = "tidyverse2019", janitor = "R-janitor", png = "R-png",
              modelbased = "modelbasedPackage", marginaleffects = "marginaleffects2024",

              brms = "brms2017", cmdstanr = "R-cmdstanr", cogmod = "R-cogmod",
              ordbetareg = "R-ordbetareg", bayestestR = "bayestestR2019",

              quanteda = "quanteda2018", quanteda.textstats = "R-quanteda.textstats",

              patchwork = "R-patchwork", scales = "R-scales", knitr = "knitr2015",

bib_keys <- str_match(readLines(here::here("manuscript", "packages.bib")), "^@[A-Za-z]+\\{([^,]+),")[, 2]
stopifnot(setequal(names(cite_key), pipeline_packages), all(cite_key %in% bib_keys))

# Small helpers for this manuscript
pct  <- \(x, d = 1) paste0(fmt_num(100 * x, d), "%")
num  <- \(x, d = 0) fmt_num(x, d)
words <- c("zero", "one", "two", "three", "four", "five", "six", "seven", "eight", "nine",
           "ten", "eleven", "twelve", "thirteen", "fourteen", "fifteen", "sixteen",
           "seventeen", "eighteen", "nineteen", "twenty")
# numbers that start a sentence are spelled out (APA); here all counts up to 20
n_word <- \(n) if (n <= 20) words[n + 1] else as.character(n)
# Exclusion sentence with a count only (no participant IDs); empty if nobody excluded
excl_n <- function(tab, reason) {
  n <- nrow(tab)
  if (n == 0) return("")
  sprintf("%s %s %s and %s excluded.", str_to_sentence(n_word(n)),
          if (n == 1) "participant" else "participants", reason,
          if (n == 1) "was" else "were")
}

# BAYESIAN MODELS ---------------------------------------------------------------------
# Results of the three Bayesian analysis documents (analysis/prequestions.qmd,
# analysis/final_test.qmd, analysis/eye_tracking.qmd), combined: tables with the same
# name are stacked (they carry a `model` column); the rest are taken as they are
bayes <- local({
  r <- map(c("prequestions", "final_test", "eye_tracking"),
           \(x) readRDS(here::here("analysis", sprintf("results_%s.rds", x))))
  out <- list()
  for (x in r) for (nm in names(x)) {
    out[[nm]] <- if (is.data.frame(x[[nm]]) && !is.null(out[[nm]])) bind_rows(out[[nm]], x[[nm]])
                 else if (is.null(out[[nm]])) x[[nm]] else out[[nm]]
  }
  out
})
```

```{r}
#| label: bayes-helpers
#| include: false
# Posterior summaries for the text and tables. Durations were modelled in s/word and are
# reported in ms per word; probabilities and proportions in percent.
b_scale <- c(total_fix = 1000, first_pass = 1000, reread_time = 1000, regressed_in = 100,
             final_test = 100)
b_unit  <- c(total_fix = "ms per word", first_pass = "ms per word",
             reread_time = "ms per word", regressed_in = "percentage points",
             final_test = "percentage points")
est_col <- \(x) intersect(c("Mean", "Difference", "Probability", "Median"), names(x))[1]

# One comparison a - b: pooled models compare statuses ("Prequestioned",
# "Non-prequestioned", "Control"); within a topic (tp), the Condition x Topic models
# compare conditions ("Polio", "TB", "Control"). Comparisons saved the other way round
# are reversed.
BY_row <- function(mod, a, b = "Control", par = "mu") {
  e <- filter(bayes$est, model == mod, parameter == par)
  sgn <- 1
  r <- filter(e, Level1 == a, Level2 == b)
  if (nrow(r) == 0) {
    r <- filter(e, Level1 == b, Level2 == a)
    sgn <- -1
  }
  f <- filter(bayes$bf, model == mod, parameter == par,
              comparison == paste(r$Level1, "-", r$Level2))
  stopifnot(nrow(r) == 1, nrow(f) == 1)
  k <- sgn * (if (par == "hu") 100 else b_scale[[mod]])
  tibble(est = k * r[[est_col(r)]], lo = min(k * r$CI_low, k * r$CI_high),
         hi = max(k * r$CI_low, k * r$CI_high), pd = r$pd, BF10 = f$BF10, BF01 = f$BF01)
}
# Group x Topic models: Polio - TB within a group ("Polio", "TB", "Control"), or the
# interaction contrast ("Interaction": the Polio group's Polio - TB minus the TB group's)
gt_lab <- \(grp) if (grp == "Interaction") "Interaction (Polio group - TB group)" else
  paste0("Polio - TB (", grp, " group)")
GT_row <- function(mod, grp, par = "mu") {
  e <- filter(bayes$est_topic, model == mod, parameter == par, comparison == gt_lab(grp))
  f <- filter(bayes$bf_topic, model == mod, parameter == par, comparison == gt_lab(grp))
  stopifnot(nrow(e) == 1, nrow(f) == 1)
  k <- if (par == "hu") 100 else b_scale[[mod]]
  tibble(est = k * e$Mean, lo = k * e$CI_low, hi = k * e$CI_high, pd = e$pd,
         BF10 = f$BF10, BF01 = f$BF01)
}
# Predicted sign of Polio - TB: positive in the Polio group and for the interaction,
# negative in the TB group (no prediction for Control)
gt_sign <- c(Polio = 1, TB = -1, Interaction = 1)
GT_pos <- \(mod, grp, par = "mu") { r <- GT_row(mod, grp, par); gt_sign[[grp]] * r$est > 0 && r$pd > 0.95 }
fmt_BF <- function(bf) {
  if (bf >= 1000) {
    e <- floor(log10(bf))
    sprintf("%s × 10^%d^", fmt_num(bf / 10^e, 1), e)
  } else if (bf >= 100) fmt_num(bf, 0) else fmt_num(bf, 2)
}
# BF10 when the evidence favours a difference, BF01 when it favours none
bf_txt <- \(r) if (r$BF10 >= 1) paste("BF~10~ =", fmt_BF(r$BF10)) else paste("BF~01~ =", fmt_BF(r$BF01))
pd_txt <- \(pd) if (pd >= 0.9995) "pd > 99.9%" else paste0("pd = ", fmt_num(100 * pd, 1), "%")
row_txt <- function(r, unit) {
  sprintf("%s %s, 95%% CrI [%s, %s], %s, %s", fmt_num(r$est, 1), unit,
          fmt_num(r$lo, 1), fmt_num(r$hi, 1), pd_txt(r$pd), bf_txt(r))
}
BY_txt <- function(mod, a, b = "Control", par = "mu") {
  row_txt(BY_row(mod, a, b, par), if (par == "hu") "percentage points" else b_unit[[mod]])
}
GT_txt <- function(mod, grp, par = "mu") {
  row_txt(GT_row(mod, grp, par), if (par == "hu") "percentage points" else b_unit[[mod]])
}
# Within-group Polio - TB differences compare different sentences (or questions), so they
# are described (estimate and 95% CrI) but not tested; the interaction contrast is tested
GT_ci <- function(mod, grp, par = "mu") {
  r <- GT_row(mod, grp, par)
  sprintf("%s %s, 95%% CrI [%s, %s]", fmt_num(r$est, 1),
          if (par == "hu") "percentage points" else b_unit[[mod]], fmt_num(r$lo, 1), fmt_num(r$hi, 1))
}
# Evidence category of a Bayes factor [@leewagenmakers2014]
bf_strength <- function(bf) {
  b <- max(bf, 1 / bf)
  if (b > 100) "extreme" else if (b > 30) "very strong" else if (b > 10) "strong" else
    if (b > 3) "moderate" else "anecdotal"
}
B_ev <- \(...) bf_strength(BY_row(...)$BF10)
# Effect present: pd > 95% in the predicted (positive) direction; Bayes factors describe
# the strength of the evidence but are not a criterion
B_pos <- \(...) { r <- BY_row(...); r$est > 0 && r$pd > 0.95 }
B_bf10 <- \(...) BY_row(...)$BF10

# Model-estimated means: by status (pooled) or by condition within a topic
B_mean <- function(mod, lvl, par = "mu", tp = NULL, d = 1) {   # tp: by group (lvl) within topic tp
  m <- if (is.null(tp)) filter(bayes$means, status == lvl)
       else filter(bayes$means_topic, condition == lvl, topic == tp)
  m <- filter(m, model == mod, parameter == par)
  stopifnot(nrow(m) == 1)
  v <- b_scale[[mod]] * m$Mean
  if (b_scale[[mod]] == 100) paste0(fmt_num(v, d), "%") else paste(fmt_num(v, d), "ms per word")
}

# Prequestions: TB - Polio (ordered beta)
PQB_mean <- \(cnd) {
  m <- filter(bayes$preq_means, condition == cnd)
  pct(m[[est_col(m)]])
}
# Described, not tested: each condition answered its own five questions, so the
# comparison is also one between two sets of questions
pq_row <- local({
  d <- bayes$preq_diff
  tibble(est = 100 * d[[est_col(d)]], lo = 100 * d$CI_low, hi = 100 * d$CI_high, pd = d$pd,
         lab = paste(d$Level1, "−", d$Level2))
})
PQB_diff <- sprintf("%s: %s percentage points, 95%% CrI [%s, %s], %s", pq_row$lab,
                    fmt_num(pq_row$est, 1), fmt_num(pq_row$lo, 1), fmt_num(pq_row$hi, 1),
                    pd_txt(pq_row$pd))

# Sampling diagnostics
diag_ok <- sum(bayes$diag$divergences) == 0 && max(bayes$diag$max_rhat) < 1.01

# Posterior figures: draws of the model-estimated means, pooled (by status) and within
# each topic (by condition, coloured by the status of the cell)
status_cols <- c(Prequestioned = "#E69F00", `Non-prequestioned` = "#56B4E9",
                 Control = "#999999")
post_plot <- function(keys, labels, unit_word) {
  topic_lab <- c(Polio = "Polio", TB = "TB")
  stat_lab <- c(Prequestioned = "Preq.", `Non-prequestioned` = "Non-preq.", Control = "No-preq.")
  cols <- c("Both topics (pooled)", "Polio group", "TB group", "No-prequestion group")
  d <- bind_rows(
    bayes$means_draws |>
      mutate(col = cols[1], x = stat_lab[as.character(status)]),
    bayes$means_topic_draws |>
      mutate(col = if_else(condition == "Control", "No-prequestion group", paste(condition, "group")),
             x = topic_lab[as.character(topic)])) |>
    # one key per plotted quantity: total_fix_mu / total_fix_tau, otherwise the model's
    # main quantity ("mu"; for the hurdle model, the expected re-reading time)
    mutate(key = if_else(model == "total_fix" | parameter != "mu",
                         paste(model, parameter, sep = "_"), model)) |>
    filter(key %in% keys) |>
    mutate(value = b_scale[model] * value,
           row = factor(labels[key], levels = labels[keys]),
           col = factor(col, levels = cols),
           x = factor(x, levels = c(stat_lab, topic_lab)),
           status = factor(status, levels = names(status_cols)))
  ggplot(d, aes(x, value, fill = status)) +
    ggdist::stat_halfeye(.width = c(0.66, 0.95), point_interval = "mean_qi",
                         slab_alpha = 0.85, point_size = 1.4, interval_size_range = c(0.5, 1.2)) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = status_cols, name = "Status of the material for the reader",
                      labels = c(Prequestioned = "Prequestioned", `Non-prequestioned` = "Non-prequestioned",
                                 Control = "No-prequestion")) +
    facet_grid(row ~ col, scales = "free", space = "free_x", switch = "y") +
    labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
    theme(legend.position = "top", panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
          panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(), strip.placement = "outside",
          strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"), panel.spacing.x = unit(1.2, "lines"),
          axis.text.x = element_text(size = 7.5, lineheight = 0.9))
}
```

The idea that learning should be error-free and effortless, while intuitive, runs counter to decades of research at the interface of cognitive science and education. Making learning more effortful, and even more error-prone, can be highly beneficial for long-term retention [@bjork1994]. This concept of *desirable difficulties* has inspired a large literature examining which learning techniques enhance memory and the mechanisms that underlie their benefits.

One of the most widely studied techniques is testing. Testing not only reveals gaps in knowledge to students and teachers, it also potentiates learning: retrieving studied information improves later memory more than restudying it does [@carpenter2012; @dunlosky2013; @kornell2016; @roediger2006; @rowland2014]. This *testing effect*, or retrieval practice effect, is robust and has been found across many types of materials and contexts.

Attempting to retrieve information can also help *before* that information has been studied. In a typical prequestion study [e.g., @richland2009], learners are assigned to a prequestion group or a control group that receives no prequestions. The prequestion group first answers questions before a learning event and is encouraged to give its best guess even when the answers are unknown; the control group begins the learning event without answering any questions. After the learning event, both groups take a final test, which includes the questions that were prequestioned for the prequestion group and new, non-prequestioned questions. The typical finding is that the prequestion group remembers the prequestioned information better than the control group does—the *prequestion effect*. Because this benefit is specific to the information targeted by the prequestions, it is often called the *specific benefit* of prequestions [@pan2023]. Prequestions sometimes also improve memory for information they did not address, a *general benefit*, but general benefits are typically smaller and appear to depend on the materials, such as short lecture videos [@carpenter2017], on the kinds of questions used [@sthilaire2019; @bostan2026], and on where untested information appears relative to the tested information [@sana2023]. Two recent meta-analyses confirmed a robust specific benefit [*g* = 0.54, @sthilaire2023; *g* = 0.66, @kingshepard2025] but found no reliable general benefit; in the larger, multilevel analysis, the general benefit was essentially zero [*g* = 0.01, @kingshepard2025]. The specific benefit, in contrast, has been replicated with prose passages [@richland2009] and video-recorded lectures [@carpenter2017; @sthilaire2020], and has been examined in classroom settings, with mixed results [@carpenter2018; @geller2017; see @pan2023 for a review].

How exactly do prequestions benefit learning? Several mechanisms have been proposed—attention, elaboration, curiosity, and metacognition—and because they are not mutually exclusive, isolating any one of them is difficult [@kingshepard2025]. They are also likely to interact: curiosity, for example, would likely increase attention to specific information, and becoming aware of a knowledge gap may make learners more curious and therefore more attentive. Attention may thus be a common route through which the other mechanisms operate, and the meta-analytic evidence aligns best with an attention-based explanation [@kingshepard2025]. On this *selective-attention* account, prequestions signal what is likely to be important on an upcoming test, so learners invest more processing in the information the prequestions address—for example, by searching for the answers and dwelling on them when they find them—and that information is remembered better because it received more attention during learning [for a review of answer-search and attentional accounts, see @pan2023]. A related attentional-window account adds that this heightened attention lasts only until the answers are found [@sana2023]. On this account, the effect of prequestions is time-limited: once the answer to a prequestion has been found, attention is no longer heightened, so information that comes afterwards receives no general benefit. @sana2023 tested this by manipulating where the prequestioned information appeared in the text. When it came at the beginning, prequestions produced only a specific benefit, but when it came at the end, so that learners were still searching for the answers while reading the rest of the text, prequestions also produced a general benefit. Most of the evidence for these accounts, however, comes from what learners remember afterwards, not from how they process the material as they learn.

Eye tracking offers a direct way to test this account. It records where and for how long readers look while they read, without interrupting or otherwise altering reading, so that processing can be examined as it unfolds rather than inferred afterwards from a memory test [@rayner1998]. Its interpretation rests on the eye–mind assumption: the information a reader is fixating is the information currently being processed, so that how long and how often readers look at a part of a text reflects how much processing it receives [@justcarpenter1980; @rayner1998]. Eye movements can also separate processing when information is first encountered from processing when readers later return to it. For these reasons, measures of real-time processing such as eye tracking have been identified as a key direction for prequestion research [@pan2023; @kingshepard2025]. Few studies have used eye tracking to examine prequestions during reading. In an early study, readers given questions before reading re-read and processed the question-related material more carefully and read more quickly through unrelated material [@rothkopf1979]. @lewis2012 [Experiment 2] had students read a text about the humanitarian efforts of the Gates Foundation, which also described polio and tuberculosis (TB). One group read four prequestions about TB before reading (e.g., "How is tuberculosis spread through the air?"), and the other group read the passage without prequestions, while eye movements were recorded with a head-mounted eye tracker. Prequestions did not slow forward reading of the targeted sentences (e.g., "Tuberculosis is spread through the air when people who have the disease cough, sneeze, or spit"), but readers who received prequestions re-read them relatively more during first-pass reading, before moving on, and spent more time looking back to them after moving on to later parts of the passage. They also looked back somewhat more to the rest of the text. On a free-recall test, the prequestion group recalled about twice as much of the targeted information as the control group, but no more of the other information. The specific benefit thus occurred without a general benefit, and it was accompanied by a shift of attention toward prequestioned information. Because only TB was prequestioned, however, the effect of prequestions could be measured only on the TB sentences, and the absence of a general effect only on the rest of the text, so neither could be separated from the content of those particular sentences; the comparisons were also between two groups of about 21 readers, based on average reading times.

More recently, @bostan2026 gave 12 adults *integrative* prequestions—questions that require combining information from different parts of a text—before they read a passage about car brakes, and compared them with 12 adults who read without prequestions. The prequestion group made more fixations and spent more time on prequestioned sentences, and made more transitions between them, than the control group. Unlike most prequestion studies, they also found a general benefit: the prequestion group scored higher on non-prequestioned questions, even though they spent less time on non-prequestioned sentences. These findings are consistent with an attentional account, but the design had the same limitation as that of @lewis2012: one fixed set of sentences was prequestioned, so the effects could not be separated from the content of those sentences. In addition, with two prequestions and 12 readers per group, compared on participants' total fixation times and counts, the estimates are imprecise, and differences between the groups in how they read the same sentences cannot be separated from differences between the readers themselves.

Attention, however, may be a by-product of prequestions rather than what directly produces their benefit, because several findings show that prequestions can improve learning without a corresponding increase in attention to the material. Pretesting has been found to reduce mind-wandering during online lectures [@pan2020], but in a larger study, content-matched pretesting neither reduced mind-wandering nor improved learning, and interpolated testing, although it slightly reduced mind-wandering, did not improve learning either [@welhaf2022], so less mind-wandering did not translate into better learning. In a large multi-site classroom study, prequestions before online lecture videos improved learning even though students did not watch more of the videos afterwards [@motz2026]. In the eye-tracking studies reviewed above, prequestions did not slow forward reading of the prequestioned sentences; instead, readers re-read them and looked back to them [@lewis2012], and integrative prequestions improved memory for non-prequestioned information even though readers spent less time on it [@bostan2026]. To account for findings like these, @motz2026 proposed the *mental model hypothesis*: prequestions activate relevant knowledge before learning, which then facilitates the processing and encoding of related information. When learners encounter content related to the prequestions, it resonates with the activated knowledge, and once they recognize it as related, they may direct additional attention to it. On this view, attention follows recognition of related content rather than directly causing the benefit.

## The Current Study

The current study tested the selective-attention account with a design that addresses the limitations of the two previous eye-tracking studies of prequestions during reading [@lewis2012; @bostan2026]. Participants read the Gates Foundation text used by @lewis2012, which discusses efforts to eradicate two diseases, polio and tuberculosis (TB). First, unlike in previous studies, the prequestioned content was counterbalanced: two prequestion groups were prequestioned on different topics, so that the effect of prequestions could be separated from the content of the sentences. Second, the sample was substantially larger—`r n_total` participants, about `r round(mean(n_by_cond$n))` per condition—and the models included variation across sentences and test questions as well as across readers, so that the effects generalize beyond these particular items. Third, beyond average reading times, we modelled the distribution of reading times, which distinguishes slower reading overall from occasional unusually long readings. Finally, unlike the integrative prequestions of @bostan2026, each prequestion was answered by a single sentence of the text, as in @lewis2012, the kind of prequestion that typically produces a specific but not a general benefit [@sthilaire2019]. Before reading, participants answered five prequestions about polio, five prequestions about TB, or no prequestions (no-prequestion condition). Each of ten target sentences in the text contained the answer to one question. Because the Polio and TB conditions swapped which topic was prequestioned, every target sentence served as prequestioned information for one group of readers and as non-prequestioned information for another. Pooling the two prequestion conditions, reading of prequestioned sentences could therefore be compared with reading of the very same sentences without prequestions (the no-prequestion condition), with each topic contributing equally.

We examined two kinds of eye-movement measures. *Global* measures—total gaze duration, re-reading time, and second-pass regressions—reflect all processing a sentence receives, including later returns to it. The *local* measure—first-pass duration—reflects processing when a sentence is first encountered. Distinguishing the two indicates *when* prequestions change processing: as readers first encounter the answer, or when they return to it later.

Fixation and reading times are not normally distributed: they cannot fall below zero and are strongly right-skewed, with a long tail of unusually long readings [@balota2011; @staub2010]. Analyses that assume normality therefore misdescribe them, and transforming the data to reduce the skew changes the hypotheses being tested [@lo2015]. We therefore analysed total gaze duration with the ex-Gaussian distribution, which describes durations as the sum of a Gaussian component, with mean μ, and an exponential component, with mean τ, and so models the skew directly. Beyond fitting the shape of the data, the ex-Gaussian has a second advantage: it separates two ways in which reading times can change, a shift of the whole distribution (μ) and a lengthening of its tail (τ), which an analysis of means cannot tell apart. Although the ex-Gaussian is a descriptive model of response times, its parameters have often been mapped onto cognitive processes, though these mappings remain debated [@matzke2009]. The Gaussian component (μ) is typically linked to relatively automatic, early-stage processing, whereas the exponential component (τ) is linked to later, more controlled processes such as attentional control, working memory updating, error monitoring, and strategic processing. In eye-tracking research on reading, word frequency affects τ as well as μ of fixation durations [@staub2010], whereas a modest degradation of the text, such as presenting it faintly, shifts only μ [@white2012]; in scene viewing, the type of image shifts μ, whereas familiarity with the image lengthens only a subset of relatively long fixations, increasing τ [@guy2020]. Some manipulations, then, lengthen a subset of unusually long fixations rather than shifting the whole distribution. Previous eye-tracking studies of prequestions analysed average reading or fixation times [@lewis2012; @yang2021; @bostan2026]. Averages can mask effects of this kind: if prequestions add processing to only some encounters with a sentence, the mean changes little, and a longer tail cannot be distinguished from slower reading overall [@guy2020]. Here, sentences that readers recognize as answering a prequestion may trigger reanalysis or additional processing. If so, prequestion effects should appear primarily in τ rather than μ. Because μ and τ are both parameters of the ex-Gaussian model, we examined both: an effect on μ would indicate that prequestions shift typical reading of the prequestioned sentences as a whole, whereas an effect on τ would indicate that they lengthen only a subset of readings, the unusually long ones, consistent with additional processing on some encounters.

### Hypotheses

For final test performance, we compared memory for prequestioned and for non-prequestioned material with memory for the same material in the no-prequestion condition, overall and on each topic. We predicted a specific benefit—better performance than the no-prequestion condition on the prequestioned topic—but no general benefit on the non-prequestioned topic.

For eye movements, we predicted a specific effect: prequestioned information would receive longer gaze durations and longer re-reading than non-prequestioned information and than the same information read without prequestions (the no-prequestion condition). Broken down by topic, readers given Polio prequestions should spend longer on Polio than on TB sentences, readers given TB prequestions should show the reverse pattern, and no-prequestion readers should show no difference between the two topics.

# Method

We report how we determined our sample size, all data exclusions (if any), all manipulations, and all measures in the study. The study was preregistered (https://osf.io/8env4). All data, materials, and analysis scripts and code are available at https://github.com/jgeller112/Prequestions_EyeTracking; every number, table, and figure in this article is computed from the raw data by the code in that repository.

## Participants

The target sample size was based on the specific benefit of prequestions. A recent meta-analysis reported a medium-sized specific benefit (*g* = 0.54; @sthilaire2023), corresponding to an odds ratio of 2.66. A simulation-based power analysis with mixedpower [@kumle2021] for the preregistered binomial mixed model, based on pilot data, indicated that 45 participants per group would provide 90% power to detect an effect of this size. We therefore planned to test 45 participants in each of the three conditions (135 in total). 

Participants were recruited from the Boston College SONA subject pool and received course credit. Eye-tracking data were recorded from `r n_recordings` participants. `r excl_n(excluded_incomplete, "had eye-tracking data for fewer than all four pages of the text")` `r excl_n(excluded_calibration, "did not meet the preregistered calibration criterion (accuracy and precision of 0.5° or better) or could not be calibrated")` `r excl_n(excluded_no_pretest, "were in a prequestion condition but had no prequestion responses")` `r excl_n(excluded_no_test, "had no final test data")` The final sample comprised `r n_total` participants (no prequestions: `r n_by_cond$n[1]`; Polio prequestions: `r n_by_cond$n[2]`; TB prequestions: `r n_by_cond$n[3]`). `r if (calib_n == n_total) 'Calibration validation data were available for all included participants.' else sprintf('Calibration validation data were available for %d of the %d included participants.', calib_n, n_total)` Mean accuracy was `r num(calib_summary$accuracy_M, 2)`° (*SD* = `r num(calib_summary$accuracy_SD, 2)`, range `r num(calib_summary$accuracy_min, 2)`–`r num(calib_summary$accuracy_max, 2)`), and mean precision (*SD* of gaze samples) was `r num(calib_summary$precision_M, 2)`° (*SD* = `r num(calib_summary$precision_SD, 2)`, range `r num(calib_summary$precision_min, 2)`–`r num(calib_summary$precision_max, 2)`). `r if (nrow(calib_over) == 0) 'All included participants with calibration data met the criterion.' else sprintf('%d participants exceeded the preregistered criterion of 0.5° (%s) and were retained.', nrow(calib_over), paste(sprintf('accuracy %s°, precision %s°', num(calib_over$accuracy, 2), num(calib_over$precision, 2)), collapse = '; '))` The preregistered exclusion of participants with high prior knowledge was not applied.

## Materials

Participants read a `r num(n_words_passage)`-word, multi-topic text [@lewis2012] that discussed the Gates Foundation's humanitarian efforts in eradicating Polio and TB in the developing world. The text consisted of `r n_sentences` sentences presented over four pages, each 16–17 lines long (@fig-aois). Ten sentences served as target sentences: five about Polio (`r WT("PO")`) and five about TB (`r WT("TB")`). The Polio target sentences had a higher reading level than the TB target sentences, as measured by the Flesch–Kincaid grade level [@kincaid1975], computed with quanteda [@quanteda2018]: Polio `r TM("PO", "fk")`; TB `r TM("TB", "fk")`. Their syntactic complexity, estimated from a dependency parse with UDPipe [@straka2017; @R-udpipe] and its model of the English Web Treebank [@silveira2014], was similar: mean dependency distance [@liu2008], the average number of words between each word and its syntactic head (Polio `r TM("PO", "mdd", 2)`; TB `r TM("TB", "mdd", 2)`), and number of clauses per sentence (Polio `r TM("PO", "clauses")`; TB `r TM("TB", "clauses")`). Each target sentence contained the answer to one of ten short-answer questions (five Polio, five TB; @apx-a). Questions were percentage-based, yes/no, or multi-part, and were worth `r points_by_topic$points[1]` points per topic (`r sum(points_by_topic$points)` points in total).

There were three conditions. In the Polio prequestion condition, participants answered the five Polio questions before reading; in the TB prequestion condition, they answered the five TB questions; in the no-prequestion condition, they read the text without prequestions. For each prequestion condition, its five target sentences were *prequestioned* and the other topic's five were *non-prequestioned*, so every target sentence served in both roles across conditions.

## Apparatus

Eye movements were recorded with a Tobii Pro Spectrum eye tracker sampling at 600 Hz. The text was displayed on an EIZO FlexScan EV2451 monitor (23.8-inch, 1920 × 1080 pixels) viewed from approximately 65 cm, without a chin rest. The text was displayed in 36-point Courier New, a monospaced font, on a grey background. At this distance, one character subtended approximately 0.5° of visual angle and one line spacing approximately 1.1°.

The whole experiment was run in Tobii Pro Lab (version 25.19). The prequestions, distractor task, and final test were PsychoPy tasks hosted on Pavlovia and presented as web elements within the Tobii Pro Lab timeline.

## Procedure

At the start of the session, each participant was randomly assigned to one of the three conditions (Polio prequestions, TB prequestions, or no prequestions). The session had four phases—prequestions, reading, a distractor task, and the final test—and participants in the no-prequestion condition skipped the first.

### Prequestions

Participants in the two prequestion conditions answered the five short-answer questions on their topic (Polio or TB), in a random order (https://run.pavlovia.org/Jgeller112/preq). They were told that they might not know the correct answers but should give their best guess. Each question was shown on the screen with a box below it, into which participants typed their response. They had unlimited time and pressed a triangle at the bottom of the screen when they were finished. No feedback was given.

### Reading

Before reading, the eye tracker was calibrated with Tobii Pro Lab's 9-point calibration procedure (white targets on a grey background), and calibration accuracy and precision were validated and recorded. Participants then read the text, presented over four pages, while their eye movements were recorded.

### Distractor Task

After reading, all participants completed the president recognition task (https://run.pavlovia.org/Jgeller112/preq_president), a distractor task lasting approximately 3 minutes.

### Final Test

Participants then answered all ten final-test questions—five on Polio and five on TB—in a random order (https://run.pavlovia.org/Jgeller112/preQ_test), in the same format as the prequestions, with unlimited time and no feedback. For participants in the prequestion conditions, five of the questions were the prequestions they had answered before reading, and five were new. Finally, participants were thanked and debriefed.

## Scoring

Prequestion and final test responses were scored by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic; model ID `claude-opus-5-5`). Rather than judging responses one at a time, Claude wrote a deterministic, rule-based scoring script (`scoring_rubric.R`, with `grade_prequestions.R` and `grade_test.R`) that awarded one point for each element of the correct answer present in a response, and applied it identically to every response. The scoring rules for each question are given in @apx-a. To check the automated scoring, a research assistant who was blind to condition, test phase, and the automated scores independently scored all `r format(rater$overall$n, big.mark = ',')` responses that were not blank. The two scorings agreed exactly on `r pct(rater$overall$exact)` of responses, and agreement was excellent, ICC(2,1) = `r sub('^0', '', fmt_num(rater$overall$icc, 2))`, 95% CI [`r sub('^0', '', fmt_num(rater$overall$icc_lo, 2))`, `r sub('^0', '', fmt_num(rater$overall$icc_hi, 2))`], using a two-way random-effects, absolute-agreement, single-rater ICC [@shrout1979; @koo2016]. For participants' final test totals, ICC(2,1) = `r sub('^0', '', fmt_num(rater$totals$icc, 2))`. Agreement for each question is given in @tbl-scoring. All analyses used the automated scores.

## Eye-Movement Data Processing

```{r}
#| label: drift-example
#| include: false
# Example reader (drift_id, fx_drift) and drift statistics (drift_stats, drift_ex):
# data/derived/manuscript_inputs.rds
drift_panel <- function(yvar, svar, title) {
  ggplot(fx_drift, aes(x, 1 - .data[[yvar]])) +
    annotation_raster(img2, 0, 1, 0, 1) +
    geom_rect(data = targets2, inherit.aes = FALSE,
              aes(xmin = x0, xmax = x1, ymin = 1 - y1, ymax = 1 - y0),
              fill = NA, colour = "grey20", linewidth = 0.3, linetype = "dashed") +
    geom_path(colour = "grey35", alpha = 0.45, linewidth = 0.25) +
    geom_point(aes(size = duration, colour = factor(.data[[svar]], levels = 1:11),
                   shape = reading), stroke = 0.6, alpha = 0.85) +
    scale_shape_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = 16, `FALSE` = 1), guide = "none") +
    scale_colour_manual(values = sentence_cols,
                        na.value = "grey55", name = "Sentence", drop = FALSE) +
    scale_size_area(max_size = 2.6, name = "Duration (ms)") +
    scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), expand = c(0, 0)) +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), expand = c(0, 0)) +
    coord_fixed(9 / 16) +
    labs(title = title) +
    theme_void(base_size = 9) +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 9, face = "bold"))
}
```

Sentence-level measures were computed from the fixation-level data rather than taken from Tobii Pro Lab's sentence metrics, for two reasons. First, when a page appeared, readers' eyes typically landed partway down the page before moving to the first line, (on `r pct(landed_below, 0)` of pages, the first fixation on the text fell below the first sentence), so Tobii Pro Lab treated the sentences above the landing point as already passed and recorded no first-pass reading for them. Second, recorded gaze positions were often offset vertically by up to about half a line, so fixations were sometimes assigned to the sentence on a neighbouring line.

Fixations were identified with Tobii Pro Lab's Tobii I-VT (Fixation) filter, a velocity-threshold identification algorithm [@salvucci2000; @olsen2012], with the following settings. Gaps in the gaze data shorter than 75 ms (e.g., brief losses of tracking) were filled by linear interpolation, the gaze positions of the two eyes were averaged, and noise was reduced with a moving median over a window of three samples. A gaze sample was classified as part of a fixation when the angular velocity of the eye, computed over a 20-ms window, was below 30°/s. Adjacent fixations separated by less than 75 ms and less than 0.5° of visual angle were merged, and fixations shorter than 60 ms were discarded. Fixations cut off when a page appeared or disappeared can nonetheless be shorter than 60 ms in the export. We excluded fixations shorter than 80 ms (`r pct(share_short)` of fixations) and longer than 1,000 ms (`r pct(share_long, 2)`) before any further processing. Both bounds follow common practice in reading research: 80 ms is the most common lower bound, and 800, 1,000, and 1,200 ms are the most common upper bounds [@schotter2025; e.g., @serranocarot2025]. Very short fixations are unlikely to reflect processing of the text and include fixations cut short by a page change. Most fixations in reading last around 200 ms [@schotter2025; @rayner1998]; in the present data the median fixation lasted `r round(fix_median)` ms, so a single fixation longer than 1,000 ms, `r fmt_num(1000 / fix_median, 1)` times the median, is unlikely to reflect ongoing reading and more likely reflects a lapse of attention or a brief loss of the eye-tracking signal that the fixation filter bridged.

The remaining processing (`derive_et_measures.R`) proceeded in four steps. (a) The exact layout of each page was reconstructed from the sentence texts and full-resolution screenshots of the pages (monospaced font, 79 characters per line), giving the screen position of every character of every sentence (@fig-aois). (b) Each fixation was assigned to a text line after correcting for vertical drift, separately for each reader and page. The correction combines two approaches used in automated drift-correction algorithms [@carr2022]: assigning sequences of fixations to a line together, and modelling drift as a function of position on the page. First, a single vertical offset was estimated: candidate shifts of the recorded positions were tried in steps of 0.05 line spacings, and the shift that minimized the summed squared distance between each fixation and its nearest text line was kept (distances were capped at one line spacing, so that stray fixations in the margins had little influence). Second, consecutive fixations moving along a line were grouped into chains; a chain ended at a horizontal jump larger than 10% of the screen width (e.g., a return sweep to the next line) or a vertical jump larger than 0.6 line spacings. Each chain was assigned as a whole to the text line nearest its median position, so that a single fixation drifting toward a neighbouring line stayed on the line being read. Third, because drift often grew down the page or across it, a linear model of the recorded vertical position as a function of the assigned line's position and the fixation's horizontal position (recorded *y* = *a* + *b* × line *y* + *c* × *x*) was fitted to fixations whose chain lay within half a line spacing of its line; gaze positions were corrected by inverting this model and the chains were reassigned, and this was repeated five times. The linear model was used only if it was plausible (a vertical stretch within 20% and a tilt of less than one line across the screen); otherwise the single offset was kept. Throughout, the correction was limited everywhere on the page to the calibration accuracy criterion of 0.5° (`r num(max_shift_cm, 2)` cm, about 0.45 of a line spacing), so it could not move a reader's gaze by a whole line. Chains more than half a line spacing from every text line were treated as off the text. (c) Each fixation was then assigned to the sentence occupying its line and horizontal position: its character column was computed from the fixed character width, a fixation on a space took the sentence of the nearest letter, and fixations more than three characters beyond either end of a line were treated as off the text. (d) Reading on each page was taken to start at the first fixation on the page's first sentence; fixations before that (the landing) contributed to total time but not to first-pass measures. After processing, `r pct(share_assigned)` of on-screen fixations were assigned to a sentence, and the assigned sentence agreed with Tobii Pro Lab's assignment for `r pct(share_agree)` of fixations. First-pass reading was identified for `r pct(fp_present_derived)` of fixated target sentences. @fig-scanpath shows one reader's fixations on one page before and after processing. For this reader, the correction moved fixations by a median of `r num(drift_ex$shift, 2)` line spacings and changed the sentence assigned to `r pct(drift_ex$relabelled)` of fixations; the medians over all readers and pages were `r num(median(drift_stats$shift), 2)` line spacings and `r pct(median(drift_stats$relabelled))`.

```{r}

Polio target sentences are shown in blue, TB target sentences in vermillion (orange-red), and other sentences in grey; numbers give each sentence's position on its page. Page 4 contains no target sentences."
#| fig-width: 6.5

wrap_plots(map(1:4, \(p) page_panel(p, label_size = 3.4)), ncol = 2, guides = "collect") &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", plot.title = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold"),
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-scanpath
#| fig-cap: "One Reader's Fixations on One Page Before and After Processing"
#| apa-note: "One participant in the TB prequestion condition, page 2, chosen to illustrate vertical drift. (A) Recorded gaze positions, coloured by the sentence assigned by Tobii Pro Lab. (B) The same fixations after drift correction (single vertical offset, assignment of chains of fixations to lines, and a linear drift model, limited to 0.5°; see Eye-Movement Data Processing), coloured by the sentence assigned in processing. Each point is one fixation (size proportional to duration); grey points were not assigned to any sentence. Lines join consecutive fixations. Open circles are fixations made before reading started on the page. Dashed rectangles outline the target sentences."
#| fig-width: 6.5
```

## Eye-Movement Measures

All measures were computed for each participant and target sentence. Durations were divided by the number of words in the sentence (ms per word), because target sentences differed in length. Only sentences that were fixated were analysed: a target sentence that received no fixation has no reading time, so its measures were treated as missing (`r n_not_fixated` of `r n_dat` target sentences, `r pct(n_not_fixated / n_dat)`). Following the eye-movement literature, we distinguish *global* measures, which reflect all processing of a sentence including later returns to it, from *local* measures, which reflect processing when the sentence is first encountered (@tbl-measures).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-measures
#| tbl-cap: "Eye-Movement Measures"
#| tbl-colwidths: [18, 9, 43, 30]
#| apa-note: "All measures were computed for each participant and target sentence. Durations were divided by the number of words in the sentence and are reported in milliseconds per word. A *pass* is a sequence of consecutive fixations on the same sentence. First-pass duration is defined only for sentences read during first-pass reading (not skipped). Global measures include later returns to the sentence; the local measure reflects processing when the sentence is first encountered."
tribble(
  ~Measure, ~Type, ~Definition, ~`Analysed as`,
  "Total gaze duration", "Global",
  "Summed duration of all fixations on the sentence.",
  "Ex-Gaussian: μ (typical reading time) and τ (tail of unusually long readings)",
  "Re-reading time", "Global",
  "Summed duration of fixations on the sentence after its first pass, that is, on returns to it (total gaze duration minus first-pass duration, excluding fixations before reading started); 0 for sentences that were not re-read. Operationalizes the preregistered re-reading measure.",
  "Hurdle Gamma: whether the sentence was re-read, and re-reading time when it was; reported as the expected re-reading time per sentence",
  "Second-pass regression (look-back)", "Global",
  "Whether the reader returned to the sentence from later text after first-pass reading had moved past it (0/1).",
  "Logistic",
  "First-pass duration", "Local",
  "Summed duration of fixations from first entering the sentence until first leaving it, provided no later sentence had been read.",
  "Gamma (log link)"
) |>
  knitr::kable(format = "pipe")
```

## Statistical Analysis

All analyses were conducted in R version `r paste(R.version$major, R.version$minor, sep = '.')` [@R-base].^[`r software_footnote`] The effects of prequestions on test performance and eye movements were estimated with Bayesian mixed models in brms [@brms2017], which fits models in Stan [@stan2017], run through cmdstanr [@R-cmdstanr] with CmdStan `r as.character(cmdstanr::cmdstan_version())`. Each target sentence, and each final-test question, was coded by its status for the reader: *prequestioned* (Polio sentences and questions for readers in the Polio condition, TB sentences and questions for readers in the TB condition), *non-prequestioned* (the other topic for those readers), or *no-prequestion* (both topics for readers in the no-prequestion condition). The main models pooled the two prequestion conditions, with Status and Topic (Polio, TB) as fixed effects. The *specific effect* of prequestions was the difference prequestioned − no-prequestion: the same sentences or questions for readers whose prequestions they answered and for readers who saw no prequestions. The *general effect* was non-prequestioned − no-prequestion. Because each topic contributes equally to the prequestioned, non-prequestioned, and no-prequestion cells, differences between the Polio and TB materials cancel in these comparisons. Both the specific and general effects and their breakdown by topic were preregistered. To break the effects down by topic, we fitted the preregistered Group (Polio prequestions, TB prequestions, or no prequestions) × Topic (Polio, TB) models with the same families and priors. Following the preregistered hypotheses, we estimated the Polio − TB difference within each group—predicted to be positive in the Polio group, negative in the TB group, and absent in the no-prequestion group—and the Group × Topic interaction contrast, the Polio group's Polio − TB difference minus the TB group's, predicted to be positive. Because the Polio and TB sentences (and questions) are different items, each within-group Polio − TB difference combines any effect of prequestions with differences between the items, and with five items per topic, the population-level topic difference is estimated imprecisely. Each within-group difference was therefore interpreted together with the interaction contrast, in which the item differences cancel because both groups read the same items.

Reading times are strongly right-skewed, so no duration was analysed with a Gaussian model. As preregistered for heavily skewed durations, total gaze duration was analysed with an ex-Gaussian distributional model (cogmod; @R-cogmod), which describes a duration as the sum of a Gaussian component, whose mean μ reflects typical reading time, and an exponential component, whose mean τ reflects the tail of unusually long readings. The fixed and random effects applied to both μ and τ, and σ had by-participant random intercepts. The ex-Gaussian could not be estimated for first-pass duration and re-reading duration: both include a large cluster of very brief readings (single short fixations on a sentence), so their distributions have no Gaussian component and its spread σ collapsed to zero. First-pass duration was therefore analysed with a Gamma model with a log link, which models positive, right-skewed durations without transforming them [@lo2015]. Re-reading duration was 0 for the `r pct(share_not_reread)` of fixated target sentences that were never re-read, which a Gamma distribution cannot produce, so it was analysed with a hurdle Gamma model. The model has two parts with the same predictors and random effects: a logistic part for whether a sentence was re-read, and a Gamma part (log link) for how long it was re-read when it was. The reported re-reading duration combines the two: the expected re-reading time per sentence, including the sentences that were not re-read. Second-pass regressions (0/1) were analysed with logistic models. Because the questions were worth different numbers of points (1–4), final test performance was analysed as the points earned on each question out of its maximum, with a beta-binomial model: a binomial model of the points earned with an additional parameter for overdispersion, because a participant tends to know all or none of a question's elements. Effects are reported on the scale of the expected proportion of a question's points, which puts all questions on the same 0–1 scale. Because each question has at most four points, scores can take only a few values (0, .25, .33, .50, .67, .75, and 1). In posterior predictive checks, the beta-binomial model reproduced how often each score occurred (predicted and observed shares within `r fmt_num(100 * max(abs(filter(bayes$score_fit, model == 'Beta-binomial')$predicted - filter(bayes$score_fit, model == 'Beta-binomial')$observed)), 1)` percentage points), better than a binomial model without overdispersion and an ordered beta model of the proportion of points [@kubinec2023; @geller2025], which placed `r pct(bayes$score_impossible[['Ordered beta']], 0)` of its predicted scores between the possible values. Prequestion performance was analysed in the same way, comparing the two prequestion conditions.

All models included the maximal random-effects structure warranted by the design [@barr2013]. Topic varied within participants, so the models included by-participant random intercepts and Topic slopes (the preregistered structure). Every target sentence and every final-test question was prequestioned for one group, non-prequestioned for another, and read or answered by the no-prequestion group, so Status (and Group) varied within items, and the models also included by-sentence (eye movements) or by-question (final test) random intercepts and Status (or Group) slopes. Within a participant, Status is determined by Topic, so no by-participant Status slope was possible. In the prequestion model, condition varied between participants and between questions, so it included random intercepts for participants and questions only. Status, Condition, and Topic were coded with equal-prior contrasts [`contr.equalprior_pairs`; bayestestR, @bayestestR2019]. With this coding, a normal(0, *s*) prior on the coefficients implies the same normal(0, *s*) prior on every pairwise difference between conditions, so that no condition serves as a reference with a different prior, and every comparison is tested against the same prior. *s* was set on each model's link scale: `r bayes$settings$s_logit` on the log-odds scale (second-pass regressions, final test, and prequestions; an odds ratio of `r fmt_num(exp(bayes$settings$s_logit), 1)` for one *SD*), `r bayes$settings$s_log` on the log scale of the Gamma models and on the scale of τ (a factor of about `r fmt_num(exp(bayes$settings$s_log), 2)` for one *SD*), and `r num(1000 * bayes$settings$s_mu)` ms per word for μ. Intercepts, random-effect standard deviations, and correlations had weakly informative priors (@apx-b). Each model was sampled with `r n_word(bayes$settings$chains)` chains of `r num(bayes$settings$iter - bayes$settings$warmup)` post-warm-up iterations (`r num(bayes$n_draws)` posterior draws, enough for stable Bayes factors). `r if (diag_ok) sprintf("All models converged: there were no divergent transitions, all R-hat values were below %s, and all bulk effective sample sizes exceeded %s.", fmt_num(max(bayes$diag$max_rhat) + 0.0005, 3), num(floor(min(bayes$diag$min_ess_bulk) / 100) * 100)) else stop("Revise: convergence sentence")`

Means and comparisons were computed on the response scale by averaging each posterior draw's predictions over the observed sample (modelbased with the marginaleffects backend and `estimate = "average"`), so that they incorporate the variation due to the random effects. Durations are reported in ms per word, and probabilities and proportions in percent. Effects were summarized by their posterior mean, 95% credible interval (CrI), and probability of direction (pd), the proportion of the posterior with the same sign as its median. The pd is closely related to the frequentist *p* value: for a one-tailed test, *p* ≈ 1 − pd, and for a two-tailed test, *p* ≈ 2(1 − pd), so pd > 95% corresponds to a one-tailed *p* < .05 [@makowski2019]. The predictions for the specific effects and for prequestioned versus non-prequestioned material were directional (longer reading, more regressions, better recall), so we treated such an effect as present when pd > 95% in the predicted direction. The general effects had no directional prediction, so for them we required pd > 97.5%, corresponding to a two-tailed *p* < .05. Bayes factors were not used as a decision criterion; we report them to describe the strength of the evidence for or against each effect. Because pd only indicates the direction of an effect and cannot provide evidence that an effect is absent, we also computed Bayes factors. Each Bayes factor compares a model in which the comparison equals 0 with one in which it is free, using the Savage–Dickey density ratio [@wagenmakers2010]: the posterior density of the comparison at 0 divided by its prior density at 0. The prior densities came from the same models sampled from their priors only, and both densities were computed for the comparisons on the link scale, where the equal priors apply. For τ and for the expected re-reading time, which have no single link scale, they were computed on the response scale; for the expected re-reading time, at the population level (without random effects), because averaging over random effects drawn from their priors produced prior draws too extreme for a density estimate. For the Group × Topic comparisons of look-backs and final test scores, the Bayes factors were also computed on the response scale (probabilities and proportions of points), the scale of the estimates. These comparisons involve different Polio and TB items, some of which had outcomes near 0 or 1, and for such outcomes the same comparison is much less precise in log-odds than in probability, so link-scale Bayes factors could contradict the estimates. BF~10~ > 3 indicates moderate, BF~10~ > 10 strong, BF~10~ > 30 very strong, and BF~10~ > 100 extreme evidence for a difference, and BF~01~ = 1/BF~10~ the corresponding evidence for no difference; values between 1/3 and 3 are anecdotal [@leewagenmakers2014]. Because a Bayes factor depends on the prior, all comparisons between conditions received the same prior, and we report how sensitive the posteriors were to the priors [power-scaling sensitivity; @priorsense2023].

### Deviations From the Preregistration

(a) The preregistered re-reading measure was operationalized as second-pass time, because Tobii Pro Lab's re-reading duration (go-past time minus first-pass time) mostly reflects time spent on earlier text rather than on the target sentence. (b) Measures were computed from the fixation data rather than taken from Tobii Pro Lab (see Eye-Movement Data Processing). (c) Durations were standardized by sentence length. (d) The preregistration specified frequentist mixed models. All confirmatory comparisons were instead estimated with Bayesian models and summarized by the probability of direction and Bayes factors, which can also quantify evidence for the absence of an effect. (e) The models added by-sentence (eye movements) or by-question (final test) random intercepts and Status (or Group) slopes to the preregistered by-participant intercepts and Topic slopes, giving the maximal structure warranted by the design. (f) First-pass duration and re-reading duration were analysed with Gamma and hurdle Gamma models rather than the preregistered linear mixed model, because the preregistered alternative for skewed durations, the ex-Gaussian, could not be estimated for them. (g) Final test and prequestion performance were analysed as the points earned on each question out of its maximum with beta-binomial models, rather than as points per topic. (h) The preregistered specific and general effects (prequestioned and non-prequestioned material versus the no-prequestion condition) were estimated with models that pooled the two prequestion conditions (Status and Topic as fixed effects), in addition to the preregistered Group × Topic models; in the Group × Topic models, the preregistered within-condition Polio − TB contrasts are reported together with the interaction contrast (see Statistical Analysis). (i) The preregistration listed first-pass regressions as a measure; this was an error for second-pass regressions (whether readers returned to a sentence from later text), the measure we intended and report. First-pass regression is therefore not reported; its analysis is included in the analysis code. (j) We planned to test 45 participants per condition (135 in total). After exclusions, the final sample comprised `r n_total` participants, and the conditions were not exactly equal in size (no prequestions: `r n_by_cond$n[n_by_cond$condition == 'Control']`; Polio prequestions: `r n_by_cond$n[n_by_cond$condition == 'Polio']`; TB prequestions: `r n_by_cond$n[n_by_cond$condition == 'TB']`).

```{r}
#| label: claims-check
#| include: false
# The Results text below makes some interpretive statements in words (e.g., "as
# predicted", "no general benefit"). The numbers update automatically when the data or
# models change, but the words do not. Each statement is checked here; if the data no
# longer support it, rendering stops with a message saying which sentence to revise.
claim <- function(ok, text) if (!isTRUE(ok)) stop("Revise the Results text: ", text, call. = FALSE)
gen_bf01 <- \(mod, par = "mu") BY_row(mod, "Non-prequestioned", par = par)$BF01

claim(all(preq_by_cond$pre_m < 0.25), "prequestions: 'participants knew little of the material before reading'")
claim(pq_row$pd < 0.95 && abs(pq_row$est) < 5, "prequestions: scores described as similar in the two conditions")
# final test
claim(B_pos("final_test", "Prequestioned"),
      "final test: specific benefit described as present, with strong evidence")
# general effect on the final test: present by the pd rule (pd > 97.5%) when negative (a cost);
# the text reports no general benefit; a cost by the pd rule is reported in Results only
ft_gen <- BY_row("final_test", "Non-prequestioned")
gen_cost <- ft_gen$est < 0 && ft_gen$pd > 0.975
claim(ft_gen$pd < 0.975 || gen_cost, "final test: a general *benefit* would need new text")
claim(ft_gen$BF10 < 3,
      "abstract, Discussion: 'no general benefit' and no general cost interpreted")
# re-reading, hurdle part: non-prequestioned sentences re-read more often (pd > 97.5%)
gen_hu <- with(BY_row("reread_time", "Non-prequestioned", par = "hu"), est < 0 && pd > 0.975)
claim(GT_row("final_test", "Polio")$lo > 0 && GT_row("final_test", "TB")$hi < 0 && GT_pos("final_test", "Interaction"),
      "final test, Group x Topic: each prequestion group scored relatively higher on its own topic (crossover)")
# eye movements, pooled
claim(B_pos("total_fix", "Prequestioned", par = "tau"),
      "eye movements: prequestioned sentences have a longer tail (τ)")
claim(BY_row("total_fix", "Prequestioned", par = "mu")$BF01 > 3,
      "eye movements: evidence that typical reading time (μ) did not change")
claim(B_pos("regressed_in", "Prequestioned"),
      "eye movements: readers more likely to return to prequestioned sentences")
claim(B_pos("reread_time", "Prequestioned"),
      "eye movements: more re-reading of prequestioned sentences")
claim(B_pos("reread_time", "Prequestioned", par = "hu") == FALSE && BY_row("reread_time", "Prequestioned", par = "hu")$est < 0 &&
        BY_row("reread_time", "Prequestioned", par = "hu")$pd > 0.95 && !B_pos("reread_time", "Prequestioned", par = "duration"),
      "eye movements: re-read more often, but not reliably longer once re-read")
claim(!B_pos("first_pass", "Prequestioned") && BY_row("first_pass", "Prequestioned")$BF01 > 1,
      "eye movements: first-pass duration not reliably longer")
gen_keys <- list(c("total_fix", "mu"), c("total_fix", "tau"), c("reread_time", "mu"),
                 c("regressed_in", "mu"), c("first_pass", "mu"))
gen_bfs <- map_dbl(gen_keys, \(k) gen_bf01(k[1], k[2]))
gen_pds <- map_dbl(gen_keys, \(k) BY_row(k[1], "Non-prequestioned", par = k[2])$pd)
claim(all(gen_bfs > 1) && all(gen_pds < 0.975),
      "eye movements: no general effect on any measure; Bayes factors favour its absence")

```

# Results

## Prequestion Performance

As intended, participants knew little of the material before reading. Participants in the Polio prequestion condition earned `r PQ("Polio", "pre_m")` of the available points on the prequestions (*SD* = `r PQ("Polio", "pre_sd")`) and those in the TB prequestion condition `r PQ("TB", "pre_m")` (*SD* = `r PQ("TB", "pre_sd")`). Participants attempted `r PQ("Polio", "att_m")` (Polio) and `r PQ("TB", "att_m")` (TB) of the prequestions; the rest were left blank or answered "I don't know". In a beta-binomial model of the points earned on each prequestion, with random intercepts for participants and questions, prequestion scores were similar in the two conditions (model-estimated scores: `r PQB_mean("TB")` in the TB and `r PQB_mean("Polio")` in the Polio condition), `r PQB_diff`. Because each condition answered its own five questions, this comparison cannot separate prior knowledge from the difficulty of the questions, so it is reported descriptively.

## Final Test Performance


Final test performance was analysed as the proportion of each question's points earned (@fig-test). Pooled over the two prequestion conditions, participants earned `r B_mean("final_test", "Prequestioned")` of the points on their prequestioned topic, compared with `r B_mean("final_test", "Control")` for no-prequestion participants on the same questions, a specific benefit of `r BY_txt("final_test", "Prequestioned")`: `r B_ev("final_test", "Prequestioned")` evidence for a difference. On the non-prequestioned topic they earned `r B_mean("final_test", "Non-prequestioned")`, `r if (gen_cost) "numerically slightly lower than in the no-prequestion condition" else "which did not reliably differ from the no-prequestion condition"`, `r BY_txt("final_test", "Non-prequestioned")`.`r if (gen_cost) paste0(" There was therefore no general benefit. Although the difference met the preregistered criterion (pd > 97.5%) in the direction of a cost, the Bayes factor was inconclusive, providing only ", bf_strength(gen_bf01("final_test")), " evidence for no difference, so we do not interpret it as a general cost.") else paste0(" The Bayes factor provided ", bf_strength(gen_bf01("final_test")), " evidence for no difference, so there was no general benefit.")`

In the Group × Topic model (@fig-test; Bayes factors on the response scale, see Statistical Analysis), the Polio group scored higher on Polio than on TB questions (`r B_mean("final_test", "Polio", tp = "Polio")` vs. `r B_mean("final_test", "Polio", tp = "TB")`), Polio − TB = `r GT_txt("final_test", "Polio")`, whereas the TB group scored higher on TB than on Polio questions (`r B_mean("final_test", "TB", tp = "TB")` vs. `r B_mean("final_test", "TB", tp = "Polio")`), Polio − TB = `r GT_txt("final_test", "TB")`. The no-prequestion group, which saw no prequestions, scored `r B_mean("final_test", "Control", tp = "Polio")` on Polio and `r B_mean("final_test", "Control", tp = "TB")` on TB questions, Polio − TB = `r GT_txt("final_test", "Control")``r if (GT_row("final_test", "Control")$lo > 0 || GT_row("final_test", "Control")$hi < 0) ", a difference in difficulty between the two sets of questions" else ""`. The Group × Topic interaction contrast—the Polio group's Polio − TB difference minus the TB group's—was `r GT_txt("final_test", "Interaction")`: `r bf_strength(GT_row("final_test", "Interaction")$BF10)` evidence that each prequestion group did relatively better on its own topic.

```{r}
#| label: fig-test
#| fig-cap: "Final Test Performance: Posterior Distributions of the Model-Estimated Means"
#| apa-note: "Posterior distributions of the model-estimated proportion of a question's points earned, averaged over the observed sample. Left: the status model, pooled over the two prequestion groups and both topics (prequestioned, non-prequestioned, and no-prequestion). Other panels: the Group × Topic model, for the Polio and TB questions in the Polio, TB, and no-prequestion groups; colours give the status of the questions for the readers in that group. Preq. = prequestioned; non-preq. = non-prequestioned; no-preq. = no-prequestion. Points are posterior means; thick and thin bars are 66% and 95% credible intervals."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 3.6
post_plot("final_test", c(final_test = "Final test score (%)"), "questions")
```

## Eye Movements

We first compare prequestioned and non-prequestioned sentences with the same sentences read by no-prequestion readers (@tbl-status), and then test the preregistered Group × Topic crossover (@fig-eye). @fig-eye shows the posterior distributions of the means for every measure, pooled and by group.

### Prequestioned and Non-Prequestioned Sentences Versus the No-Prequestion Condition

Prequestions changed how readers read the sentences that answered them, compared with no-prequestion readers reading the same sentences (@tbl-status). In the ex-Gaussian model of total gaze duration, prequestioned sentences had a longer tail of unusually long readings, τ: `r BY_txt("total_fix", "Prequestioned", par = "tau")`, `r B_ev("total_fix", "Prequestioned", par = "tau")` evidence for a difference. Typical reading time did not differ, μ: `r BY_txt("total_fix", "Prequestioned", par = "mu")`, with `r bf_strength(BY_row("total_fix", "Prequestioned", par = "mu")$BF10)` evidence for no difference. Readers were more likely to return to prequestioned sentences from later text (`r B_mean("regressed_in", "Prequestioned")` vs. `r B_mean("regressed_in", "Control")`), `r BY_txt("regressed_in", "Prequestioned")`, `r B_ev("regressed_in", "Prequestioned")` evidence. Prequestioned sentences also received more re-reading: the expected re-reading time per sentence, including sentences that were not re-read, was `r B_mean("reread_time", "Prequestioned")` compared with `r B_mean("reread_time", "Control")`, `r BY_txt("reread_time", "Prequestioned")`, `r B_ev("reread_time", "Prequestioned")` evidence. In the two parts of the hurdle model, this reflected re-reading more often—prequestioned sentences were `r fmt_num(-BY_row("reread_time", "Prequestioned", par = "hu")$est, 1)` percentage points more likely to be re-read (`r pd_txt(BY_row("reread_time", "Prequestioned", par = "hu")$pd)`, `r bf_txt(BY_row("reread_time", "Prequestioned", par = "hu"))`)—rather than longer re-reading once a sentence was re-read (`r sub(" percentage points", "", BY_txt("reread_time", "Prequestioned", par = "duration"))`). First-pass duration was not reliably longer, `r BY_txt("first_pass", "Prequestioned")`; the Bayes factor favoured no difference, but with only `r bf_strength(BY_row("first_pass", "Prequestioned")$BF10)` evidence.

Non-prequestioned sentences, by contrast, were read like the same sentences in the no-prequestion condition. No measure showed a general effect (non-prequestioned − no-prequestion, @tbl-status; all pd < 97.5%), and on every measure the Bayes factor favoured its absence (BF~01~ from `r fmt_num(min(gen_bfs), 1)` to `r fmt_num(max(gen_bfs), 1)`), with `r if (all(gen_bfs > 3)) "moderate or stronger evidence on every measure" else sprintf("moderate or stronger evidence for %d of the %d measures and anecdotal evidence for the rest", sum(gen_bfs > 3), length(gen_bfs))`. `r if (gen_hu) paste0("In the hurdle part of the re-reading model, non-prequestioned sentences were also somewhat more likely to be re-read than without prequestions (", fmt_num(-BY_row("reread_time", "Non-prequestioned", par = "hu")$est, 1), " percentage points, ", pd_txt(BY_row("reread_time", "Non-prequestioned", par = "hu")$pd), ", ", bf_txt(BY_row("reread_time", "Non-prequestioned", par = "hu")), "), but the expected re-reading time did not differ. ") else ""`The effects of prequestions on reading were therefore `r if (gen_hu) "largely specific" else "specific"` to the prequestioned sentences.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-status
#| tbl-cap: "Prequestioned and Non-Prequestioned Sentences Versus the Same Sentences Read Without Prequestions"
#| tbl-colwidths: [22, 21, 9, 9, 21, 9, 9]
#| apa-note: "Posterior means and 95% credible intervals of the differences, pooled over the Polio and TB prequestion conditions and averaged over the two topics, in ms per word (durations) or percentage points (second-pass regressions). Prequestioned − no-prequestion is the specific effect and non-prequestioned − no-prequestion the general effect of prequestions. Total gaze duration was analysed with an ex-Gaussian model (μ = typical reading time; τ = tail of unusually long readings); re-reading duration with a hurdle Gamma model (expected re-reading time per sentence, including sentences not re-read as 0); first-pass duration with a Gamma model; second-pass regressions with a logistic model. pd = probability of direction. BF~10~ = Bayes factor for a difference (Savage–Dickey); BF~01~ = 1/BF~10~, evidence for no difference. First-pass duration is a local measure; all others are global."
eye_keys <- tribble(
  ~mod,           ~par,  ~Measure,
  "total_fix",    "mu",  "Total gaze: μ",
  "total_fix",    "tau", "Total gaze: τ",
  "reread_time",  "mu",  "Re-reading duration",
  "regressed_in", "mu",  "Second-pass regression",
  "first_pass",   "mu",  "First-pass duration")
ci_cell <- \(r) sprintf("%s [%s, %s]", fmt_num(r$est, 1), fmt_num(r$lo, 1), fmt_num(r$hi, 1))
pd_cell <- \(r) if (r$pd >= 0.9995) "> 99.9%" else paste0(fmt_num(100 * r$pd, 1), "%")
eye_keys |>
  mutate(spec = map2(mod, par, \(m, p) BY_row(m, "Prequestioned", par = p)),
         gen  = map2(mod, par, \(m, p) BY_row(m, "Non-prequestioned", par = p))) |>
  transmute(Measure,
            `Prequestioned − No-prequestion` = map_chr(spec, ci_cell),
            pd = map_chr(spec, pd_cell),
            `BF~10~` = map_chr(spec, \(r) fmt_BF(r$BF10)),
            `Non-prequestioned − No-prequestion` = map_chr(gen, ci_cell),
            `pd ` = map_chr(gen, pd_cell),
            `BF~01~` = map_chr(gen, \(r) fmt_BF(r$BF01))) |>
  knitr::kable(format = "pipe")
```

### Group × Topic

```{r}
#| label: topic-prep
#| include: false
# Interaction contrast for each eye-movement measure: present (pd > 95%) or not
int_status <- eye_keys |>
  mutate(status = map2_chr(mod, par, \(m, p)
    if (GT_pos(m, "Interaction", p)) "pos" else "no"))
nice <- c(`Total gaze: μ` = "typical reading time (μ)", `Total gaze: τ` = "the tail of unusually long readings (τ)",
          `Re-reading duration` = "re-reading time", `Second-pass regression` = "look-backs from later text",
          `First-pass duration` = "first-pass reading")
# measures with the given status; with numbers = TRUE, each with its interaction estimate
int_list <- function(st, numbers = FALSE) {
  r <- filter(int_status, status == st)
  lab <- nice[r$Measure]
  if (numbers) lab <- sprintf("%s: %s", lab, map2_chr(r$mod, r$par, \(m, p) GT_txt(m, "Interaction", p)))
  knitr::combine_words(lab, sep = if (numbers) "; " else ", ")
}
int_summary_fun <- function(numbers) {
  parts <- c(
    if (any(int_status$status == "pos")) paste("positive (pd > 95%) for", int_list("pos", numbers)),
    if (any(int_status$status == "no")) paste("not reliably positive for", int_list("no", numbers)))
  n <- length(parts)
  if (n == 1) parts
  else if (numbers) paste(parts, collapse = ". It was ")     # two sentences
  else paste0(paste(parts[-n], collapse = "; "), "; and ", parts[n])
}
int_summary <- int_summary_fun(FALSE)          # Discussion
int_summary_num <- int_summary_fun(TRUE)       # Results, with the estimates
```

The preregistered prediction was a crossover: longer reading of Polio than of TB sentences in the Polio group, the reverse in the TB group, and no difference in the no-prequestion group, so that the Group × Topic interaction contrast would be positive. The interaction contrast was `r int_summary_num`. For the tail of total gaze duration (τ), the Polio − TB difference was `r GT_txt("total_fix", "Polio", "tau")` in the Polio group, `r GT_txt("total_fix", "TB", "tau")` in the TB group, and `r GT_txt("total_fix", "Control", "tau")` in the no-prequestion group. For look-backs from later text (Bayes factors on the response scale), it was `r GT_txt("regressed_in", "Polio")` in the Polio group, `r GT_txt("regressed_in", "TB")` in the TB group, and `r GT_txt("regressed_in", "Control")` in the no-prequestion group. Because the Polio and TB sentences differ, the no-prequestion group shows how the topics are read without prequestions (@fig-eye).

Left: the status models, pooled over the two prequestion groups and both topics (prequestioned, non-prequestioned, and no-prequestion sentences). Other panels: the Group × Topic models, for the Polio and TB sentences in the Polio, TB, and no-prequestion groups; colours give the status of the sentences for the readers in that group. μ and τ are the Gaussian mean (typical reading time) and the tail mean (unusually long readings) of the ex-Gaussian model of total gaze duration. Durations are in ms per word; second-pass regressions are the percentage of sentences returned to from later text. Preq. = prequestioned; non-preq. = non-prequestioned; no-preq. = no-prequestion. Points are posterior means; thick and thin bars are 66% and 95% credible intervals."
```{r}
#| fig-width: 6.5
```
