```{r}
post_plot(c("total_fix_mu", "total_fix_tau", "reread_time", "regressed_in", "first_pass"),
          c(total_fix_mu = "Total gaze: μ\n(ms/word)", total_fix_tau = "Total gaze: τ\n(ms/word)",
            reread_time = "Re-reading duration\n(ms/word)", regressed_in = "Second-pass\nregression (%)",
            first_pass = "First-pass duration\n(ms/word)"),
          "sentences")
```

# Discussion

This study used eye tracking to test whether prequestions improve memory by directing attention toward the information they address. Two sets of preregistered comparisons addressed this question. Pooling the two prequestion groups, we compared each target sentence and question when it answered the reader's prequestions with the same sentence or question for readers who saw no prequestions (the specific effect), and the other topic's material with the same material without prequestions (the general effect). The Group × Topic comparisons then asked whether the effects reversed with the prequestioned topic, that is, whether the Polio group favoured Polio material and the TB group TB material. On the final test, prequestions produced the typical specific benefit and no general benefit, and the crossover was clear: each prequestion group did relatively better on its own topic (interaction contrast, `r bf_strength(GT_row("final_test", "Interaction")$BF10)` evidence). Eye movements showed the same specificity. Compared with the same sentences read without prequestions, prequestioned sentences received more unusually long readings, were re-read more often, and were more likely to be looked back to from later text, whereas non-prequestioned sentences were read like the same sentences in the no-prequestion condition on every measure. In the Group × Topic comparisons, the interaction contrast was `r int_summary` (@fig-eye). Prequestions therefore changed how readers treated the information they targeted, and only that information.

The pattern of eye-movement effects indicates what kind of attention prequestions recruit. First, prequestions did not make readers read the relevant material more slowly overall: the Bayes factors favoured no difference from the no-prequestion condition in typical reading time (μ) and, more weakly, in first-pass duration. Prequestions therefore do not seem to act as a general instruction to read prequestion-relevant content with more care. Second, the additional processing appeared in a subset of encounters—as occasional unusually long readings in the tail of the reading-time distribution (τ)—and in returns to the sentences: readers re-read prequestioned sentences more often and looked back to them more often from later text, although re-reading was not reliably longer once it occurred. Third, the additional processing was confined to the prequestioned sentences: the non-prequestioned sentences, interleaved with them in the same text, were read as they were without prequestions`r if (gen_hu) ', except that they were somewhat more likely to be re-read' else ''`.`r claim(BY_row("first_pass", "Prequestioned")$BF01 > 1 && BY_row("total_fix", "Prequestioned", par = "mu")$BF01 > 3, "Discussion: Bayes factors favour no difference in μ and (more weakly) first-pass duration")`

Together, these features suggest that additional processing is triggered when a reader recognizes that a sentence answers one of the prequestions. Recognizing an answer requires matching the sentence against the prequestions held in memory, so it can occur only once enough of the sentence has been read, and it can fail—a reader may not notice the connection, or may no longer remember the question. Recognition may also be what makes prequestions effective: in video lectures, prequestions enhanced learning only when learners remembered them [@sthilaire2020]. Recognition would therefore add processing to some encounters but not others, lengthening the tail of the reading-time distribution rather than shifting the whole distribution, as the effect on τ but not μ shows. Ex-Gaussian analyses of fixation durations in reading have shown that the two components can be affected separately. Word frequency affects both μ and τ [@staub2010], whereas a modest degradation of the text, such as presenting it faintly, increases only μ, slowing all fixations by a similar amount without adding unusually long ones [@white2012]. Prequestions showed the reverse pattern: they did not shift typical reading time but lengthened only the tail. They therefore did not make the prequestioned sentences harder or slower to read in general; instead, they added processing to a subset of encounters with them. Memory-based processes have been found to act on τ in this way in scene viewing, where familiarity with an image lengthened only a subset of relatively long fixations [@guy2020]. Once an answer is recognized, readers may pause to compare it with the question or with the guess they gave before reading and to encode it in relation to the question, and they may return to it later to check or rehearse it, as the increased re-reading and look-backs suggest. Part of this pattern fits the attentional-window account [@sana2023], on which prequestions heighten attention while learners search for the answers, until the answers are found: the long readings of the answer sentences could mark the point at which a reader finds an answer. The account does not, however, predict the look-backs. Once an answer has been found, attention should return to its usual level, yet readers returned to prequestioned sentences from later text more often than no-prequestion readers returned to the same sentences. Prequestions therefore appear to engage readers with an answer beyond the moment it is found: after recognizing it, readers return to it, perhaps to check it against the question or against their earlier guess, or to rehearse it. The recognition account covers both features of the data—pausing when an answer is recognized and returning to it later—whereas the attentional-window account covers only the first.

The recognition account is also what the mental model hypothesis predicts [@motz2026]. On that hypothesis, prequestions activate relevant knowledge, information related to it resonates with that knowledge when it is encountered, and additional attention follows recognition rather than preceding it. Consistent with this sequence, prequestions here did not lengthen first-pass reading or typical reading time of the prequestioned sentences, as heightened attention from the start would; instead, they added processing once an answer had been read and drew readers back to it later. The present design, however, tests only part of the hypothesis. The non-prequestioned sentences were about the other disease, so they do not show whether activated knowledge also facilitates the processing of related, non-prequestioned information on the prequestioned topic.

The pattern also adds to evidence that attention is not the whole story. If prequestions worked simply by heightening attention to the content they address, readers should have read that content more slowly or carefully throughout, shifting the whole distribution of reading times, that is, μ. Instead, typical reading time did not change—the Bayes factor favoured no difference in μ—and prequestions lengthened only the tail of the distribution (τ) and increased returns to the answers. Together with findings that prequestions can improve learning without increasing the time spent on the material [@motz2026] and that pretesting does not always reduce mind-wandering [@welhaf2022], this suggests that heightened attention alone does not explain prequestion effects. The occasional long pauses and the returns to the answers instead resemble metacognitive monitoring. On a metacognitive account, answering prequestions shows learners what they do not know, and they then monitor the material for the information that fills these gaps [@kingshepard2025]: noticing that a sentence answers a question, comparing it with the guess given before reading, and checking it later. Recognizing an answer is itself a metacognitive judgment, so the recognition-triggered processing proposed here can be understood as metacognitive monitoring expressed in eye movements. Because monitoring is itself expressed through where and for how long readers look, eye movements alone cannot separate the two accounts. Combining eye tracking with direct measures of metacognition, such as judgments of learning or confidence in each answer, as recently recommended [@kingshepard2025], could do so.

The specificity of the effects also constrains the mechanism. A specific benefit on its own is consistent with any of the proposed mechanisms—attention, elaboration, curiosity, or metacognition—but the absence of a general benefit is not consistent with accounts on which prequestions raise curiosity or prompt metacognitive monitoring for the topic as a whole [@kingshepard2025]. In their meta-analysis, @kingshepard2025 found no general benefit, and also no general cost, which suggests that if prequestions orient attention toward the prequestioned information, this orienting does not impede learning of other information. The eye movements here fit this view: non-prequestioned sentences were read as they were without prequestions on every measure, so prequestions changed how readers treated their answers, not how they read the topic or the passage as a whole.

Whether these episodes of additional processing produce the memory benefit cannot be determined from these data. Reading was observed rather than manipulated, and the eye-movement effects were modest compared with the memory benefit, so prequestions may also strengthen memory through processes that leave little trace in reading time, such as how an answer is encoded once it is recognized or how it is related to the earlier retrieval attempt. This possibility is consistent with evidence that prequestions can improve learning without increasing the time learners spend on the material [@motz2026]. Experiments that manipulate whether and when readers can return to the answers, or that record recognition of answers directly, could test whether recognition-triggered processing is necessary for the benefit.

These findings agree with the two previous eye-tracking studies of prequestions in showing that prequestions shift attention toward the information they address. In @lewis2012, TB prequestions increased first-pass reading of the targeted sentences by increasing re-reading within those sentences before readers moved on, rather than by slowing forward reading, and increased the time spent looking back to them after moving on. Readers in both studies were more likely to look back to prequestioned sentences from later in the text. Both studies also found more time spent re-reading prequestioned sentences, although here this reflected re-reading them more often rather than for longer. The studies differ in first-pass reading, which was not reliably longer than in the no-prequestion condition here. Earlier studies also analysed average reading and fixation times, whereas the present analysis separated typical reading time (μ) from the tail of unusually long readings (τ). This distinction matters for prequestions: the extra processing here was confined to a subset of encounters, which an analysis of means would dilute and could not distinguish from slower reading overall. Several differences between the studies may contribute. @lewis2012 compared a single prequestion group with a control group of about 21 readers each, whereas the present design pooled two prequestion groups that targeted different sentences, so that every target sentence was compared with and without prequestions in a larger sample. Re-reading is also defined differently across studies and eye-tracking software; for example, re-reading duration is sometimes computed as go-past time minus first-pass time, which mostly reflects time spent on earlier text, whereas we measured re-reading as time spent on the target sentence itself after first-pass reading. Finally, we corrected for the eyes landing partway down a page when it first appears, which otherwise misclassifies the first reading of sentences near the top of a page as re-reading. @bostan2026 likewise found more fixations and longer fixation time on prequestioned sentences, and more transitions between prequestioned sentences, which parallels the look-backs we observed. Unlike the present results and most prequestion research, they also reported a general benefit. Their integrative prequestions required combining information from different parts of the text, which may have directed attention to non-prequestioned information as well, consistent with the view that general benefits arise when prequestions direct attention beyond the tested information [@pan2023]. In the present study, prequestions about single facts neither increased attention to non-prequestioned information nor improved memory for it. With 12 participants per group, however, the estimates of @bostan2026 are imprecise.

Several limitations should be noted. Each topic was represented by only five target sentences and five test questions. The within-group Polio − TB differences therefore combine any effect of prequestions with differences between the materials: the Polio and TB sentences differed in length, content, reading level, and position on the page, and the no-prequestion group read them differently even without prequestions. The Group × Topic interaction contrasts remove these differences, but they compare two groups of readers and rest on five items per topic. We therefore based our conclusions primarily on the pooled comparisons, which compare the same sentences and questions with and without prequestions, so that differences between the materials cancel out, and we treat the Group × Topic contrasts as converging evidence where they were reliable. Texts with more target sentences per topic would allow topic-specific effects to be estimated precisely. The comparisons with the no-prequestion condition are between participants, and so are less precise than comparisons within readers. The Bayes factors depend on the priors on the effects: wider priors favour the absence of an effect more strongly, and narrower priors less so. They show that the data are better described without a general effect than with an effect of the size the priors allow, not that a small general effect is impossible. Eye movements were recorded without head stabilization, and recorded gaze positions drifted vertically for some readers. The measures were therefore derived from the fixation data with a drift correction bounded by the calibration accuracy criterion; drift beyond that bound was not corrected.

In sum, prequestions guide where readers look, and only toward the information they target: rather than reading the relevant material more slowly, readers pause on some of the answers and return to them later, while reading the rest of the text as they would without prequestions. Prequestions therefore do not simply heighten attention to the material they address. Such recognition-triggered processing is a plausible route by which prequestions strengthen memory for their answers, but whether it accounts for the memory benefit remains to be tested.

# Questions and Scoring Rules {#apx-a}

Prequestion and final test responses were scored with the same rule-based script (`scoring_rubric.R`), written by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic; model ID `claude-opus-5-5`) and applied identically to every response. Each question awarded one point per correct element present in the response (@tbl-questions, @tbl-scoring). Blank responses, "I don't know" and similar responses, and random keystrokes scored 0. Minor misspellings were accepted when the intended word was unambiguous (e.g., "afganistan"). The same rules were used for the prequestions and the final test.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-questions
#| tbl-cap: "Final Test Questions and Answers"
#| tbl-colwidths: [5, 8, 45, 34, 8]
#| apa-note: "Points = maximum points for the question. The Polio prequestion condition answered questions 1–4 and 10 before reading; the TB prequestion condition answered questions 5–9."
answer_key |>
  arrange(questnum) |>
  transmute(Q = questnum, Topic = Condition, Question, Answer, Points) |>
  knitr::kable(format = "pipe")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-scoring
#| tbl-cap: "Scoring Rules and Agreement With the Second Rater for Each Question"
#| tbl-colwidths: [5, 63, 8, 12, 12]
#| apa-note: "One point was awarded for each credited element present in a response, up to the question's maximum (see Table A1). *n* = number of non-blank responses (prequestions and final test) scored by both the automated rubric and the second rater; Exact = percentage of responses given the same score; ICC = ICC(2,1), absolute agreement."
credited <- c(
  `1`  = "The number 17 (as a whole number, e.g., not 170).",
  `2`  = "A negative answer: \"no\", \"no cure\", or \"not a cure\".",
  `3`  = "One point each for Nigeria, India, Pakistan, and Afghanistan.",
  `4`  = "One point each for antibiotics; analgesics or pain relief; exercise (including physical activity or therapy); and diet or nutrition. \"Antibiotic resistance\" alone was not credited.",
  `5`  = "One point each for cough (or blood-tinged sputum/phlegm); fever (or temperature); night sweats; and weight loss.",
  `6`  = "10% (or \"ten percent\", 1/10); not credited if stated as \"less than\" or \"under\" 10%.",
  `7`  = "One point each for antibiotics (or antibacterials); two (two drugs, courses, rounds, or types); and long-term (long, extended, prolonged, or months).",
  `8`  = "A negative answer (\"no\").",
  `9`  = "One point each for cough, sneeze, and spit (or saliva).",
  `10` = "One point each for a starting value of hundreds of thousands (100,000–999,999) and an end value of about a thousand (500–9,999, or \"a thousand\")."
)
tibble(Q = 1:10, `Credited elements` = credited[as.character(1:10)]) |>
  left_join(transmute(rater$by_question, Q = as.integer(questnum), `*n*` = n,
                      Exact = paste0(fmt_num(100 * exact, 1), "%"),
                      ICC = sub("^0", "", fmt_num(icc, 2))), by = "Q") |>
  knitr::kable(format = "pipe")
```

# Model Specifications {#apx-b}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-models
#| tbl-cap: "Bayesian Models: Families, Effects, and Priors"
#| tbl-colwidths: [20, 22, 30, 28]
#| apa-note: "Pooled models: Status (prequestioned, non-prequestioned, no-prequestion) + Topic; Group × Topic models: Group (Polio, TB, no-prequestion) × Topic. Status, Condition, and Topic were coded with equal-prior contrasts, so the prior on the coefficients is also the prior on every pairwise difference between conditions (on the link scale). Other priors: intercepts normal(−1.5, 1) on the log scale (Gamma models; about 0.2 s per word), normal(0, 1.5) on the log-odds scale, and normal(0.2, 0.2) s per word for μ; ex-Gaussian σ and τ intercepts normal(−2.5, 1) on the softplus scale; random-effect *SD*s Student-*t*(3, 0, *v*) with *v* = 0.5 (Gamma models, ex-Gaussian σ and τ), 1 (logistic and beta-binomial models), or 0.1 (ex-Gaussian μ); random-effect correlations LKJ(2); the Gamma shape gamma(2, 0.5); beta-binomial overdispersion exponential(0.1). Durations were modelled in s per word."
s_tab <- bayes$settings
tribble(
  ~Measure, ~Family, ~`Random effects`, ~`Prior on comparisons`,
  "Total gaze duration", "Ex-Gaussian (μ identity; σ, τ softplus)",
  "μ and τ: participants (intercept, Topic slope), sentences (intercept, Status or Group slope); σ: participants (intercept)",
  sprintf("μ: normal(0, %s) s/word; τ: normal(0, %s)", s_tab$s_mu, s_tab$s_log),
  "First-pass duration", "Gamma (log)", "Participants (intercept, Topic slope), sentences (intercept, Status or Group slope)",
  sprintf("normal(0, %s)", s_tab$s_log),
  "Re-reading duration", "Hurdle Gamma (Gamma: log; hurdle: logit)",
  "Both parts: participants (intercept, Topic slope), sentences (intercept, Status or Group slope)",
  sprintf("Gamma: normal(0, %s); hurdle: normal(0, %s)", s_tab$s_log, s_tab$s_logit),
  "Second-pass regression", "Bernoulli (logit)", "Participants (intercept, Topic slope), sentences (intercept, Status or Group slope)",
  sprintf("normal(0, %s)", s_tab$s_logit),
  "Final test", "Beta-binomial (logit)", "Participants (intercept, Topic slope), questions (intercept, Status or Group slope)",
  sprintf("normal(0, %s)", s_tab$s_logit),
  "Prequestions", "Beta-binomial (logit)", "Participants (intercept), questions (intercept)",
  sprintf("normal(0, %s)", s_tab$s_logit)
) |>
  knitr::kable(format = "pipe")
```
